figures.caption: Figure 1: Example illustrating equivariant model selection for binary datasets ŝ = {s(i)}N i=1, where each datapoint s(i) is a state of a three-spin system s = (s1, s2, s3) ∈ {−1,+1}3. A model selection procedure is equivariant if, for a basis transformation of the dataset T : s → σ, the models obtained from the model selection procedure on ŝ (Bob’s data) and σ̂ (Alice’s data) are related by the same transformation T . The left panel shows an example of an equivariant model selection procedure, for which the spin model found in Alice’s data representation corresponds to the model found in Bob’s representation rewritten in Alice’s basis, i.e. MAlice = T [MBob]. In the right panel, Alice and Bob have the same data as in the left panel, but they can only select among pairwise models. In this case, Bob will find the same model as in the left panel because his model is already pairwise, but Alice’s model cannot be the same because her model has a three body interaction. Instead, Alice will find a pairwise model that likely has similarities with her left-panel model (such as the projection of the three-body interaction onto pairwise interactions), but which cannot be consistent with Bob’s findings anymore. This gives an example where it is clear that pairwise model selection is not equivariant.

Figure 7: Illustration: Representation of q-state spin models as linear maps. We consider a system with n q-state spin variables and a spin model M with K operators. The space V = (Z/qZ)n (on the right) is the system space, in which each of the n basis elements is associated with one of the spin variables. The state of the system is then represented by the random vector α = (α1, . . . , αn) ∈ V, where αj is the color of the j-th spin, and a spin operator is represented as a vector µ ∈ V, which gives the decomposition of the operator in terms of the variables of the system. The space U = (Z/qZ)K (on the left) is the model space, in which each of the K basis elements is associated with one of the operators of the model (which are the variables of the models). The state of the model is then represented by the random vector m = (m1, . . . ,mK) ∈ U , where mk is the color of the k-th operator, ϕuk (m) = zmk q , and each spin operator that can be decomposed over the operators of the model is represented by a vector u ∈ U . A model M is represented by a linear map fM that associates each operator represented by u ∈ U in model space to a representation µ = fM(u) ∈ V in system space. The map fM is defined in Eq. (106) by specifying the image µk = fM(uk) ∈ V of each basis vector uk ∈ U . Gauge transformations T are automorphisms of V. Loops of M correspond to the vectors ℓ ∈ U whose image is the null vector fM(ℓ) = 0 ∈ V.

Figure 8: (colors online) Visualization of MCMs as factorization in state space. Left. In each row, the left panel shows an MCM based on four discrete variables (α1, α2, α3, α4) with two ICCs represented in different colors. The MCM is represented in a preferred basis, which means that each ICC contains all possible operators over the shown subset of α-variables. The value of q for the discrete variables is not yet specified and the diagrams can be read for any chosen value of q. For example, for the top row: for q = 2, the red ICC has the q2 − 1 = 3 operators (µ1, µ2) ∈ {(1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)}; for q = 3, the red ICC has the q2 − 1 = 8 operators (µ1, µ2) ∈ {(1, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 1), (2, 2), (1, 2), (2, 1)}. Right. The panel represents the factorization in state space (for q = 2 and q = 3) that results from the MCM partition of the basis variables αi shown in the left panel. The model probability distribution can be written as the product of joint distributions over lower dimensional subspaces shown in colors (line, surface, or volume). The color (green or red) refers to the corresponding ICC in the left panel and each marker represents a state of the system reduced to these subspaces (e.g., for the top panel and q = 2, the pair of variables (α1, α2) can take the values {(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)}, hence the four markers in the red area). The probability of the states that are not represented by a colored marker is obtained by products of the probabilities of the sub-states that are represented by a marker. When written in a preferred basis, the factorization of the state space resulting from the same MCM partition of the basis variables into ICC (as in the left panel) doesn’t depend on the value of the discretization q of the variables. The only difference is the increase of the number of states in each subspace with q.

Figure 9: Examples of MCMs and their GTs to a preferred basis. Each box contains an example of an MCM. Operators are represented using the same convention as in Fig. 6. In panel b), the green color is also used to indicate that a spin is raised to the third power in the corresponding operator (e.g., in model M, the green pairwise link represents the operator s 3 1 s 3 2 ). For each example, we use the GT T to transform the top model into the bottom one, and the inverse GT T −1 to go back to the top model. The bottom model M′ is in a preferred basis, in which each ICC appears in a compact complete form over a subset of spins (circled with gray dashed lines). The matrix representations of these models and of their GTs are available in App. D.1. a) Example of two equivalent MCMs with q = 3 for n = 3 spins; these models have two ICCs with rank 2 and 1 respectively. For clarity we represented the models using the decomposition M = M1 ∪ M∗ 1, where the operators in M∗ 1 are the c.c. of the operators in M1. The transformed model is obtained using M′ = M′ 1 ∪ M∗′ 1 , where M′ 1 = T [M1] (see Sec. 4.4). b) Example of two equivalent MCMs, M and M′, with q = 4 for n = 2 spins; these models have a single ICC of rank 1.

Figure 10: (colors online) Representation of the model discrete probability distribution in state space for two ICCs of Fig. 9. Each dot represents a state of the spin system and the color represents the probability of the state. States with the same color have the same probability. Top panel. Representation of the probability distribution of the MCM with a single ICC in Fig. 9.b. In the best basis, defined as the color variables (α′ 1, α ′ 2) in the bottom panel of Fig. 9.b, one can see directly that the model probability distribution factorizes and is uniform along the direction of α′ 2, which gives the state space representation in the top left panel. After the GT (α1, α2) = T −1[(α′ 1, α ′ 2)] (top MCM in Fig. 9.b), the probability distribution remains uniform in the direction of α′ 2, which is perpendicular to the direction of α′ 1 = α1 + α2. This is a nontrivial factorization when looking at the system of variables (α1, α2). Bottom panel. Representation of the probability distribution of the single ICC based on the spin variables (σ1, σ2) in the bottom panel of Fig. 9.a. We denote by (α′ 1, α ′ 2, α ′ 3) the corresponding color variables of this basis, which is a preferred basis for the ICC, and by (α1, α2, α3) the basis variables for the top panel of Fig. 9.a. Independently of the basis representation, the probability distribution for this ICC is uniform in the direction of α′ 3 (indicated here by the color remaining identical in this direction), which is perpendicular to the plane defined by α′ 1 and α′ 2. The independencies in the model probability distribution (here indicated by the uniform direction) are non-trivial in the basis of the variables (α1, α2, α3) (bottom right panel), but much easier to see in the basis of the variables (α′ 1, α ′ 2, α ′ 3) (bottom left panel).

Figure 12: MCM analysis of the US Supreme Court data in its original basis for different embeddings. The original dataset is binary and is embedded in the larger q-state space for this analysis. Top. Optimal MCM found by exhaustive search in the original basis of the data for different values of q. The circles represent the 9 justices labeled by their initials: Ruth Bader Ginsburg (RG), John P. Stevens (JS), David Souter (DS), Stephen Breyer (SB), Sandra Day O’Connor (SO), William Rehnquist (WR), Anthony Kennedy (AK), Clarence Thomas (CT), and Antonin Scalia (AS). MCMs are represented as partitions of the basis variables, with components identified by different colors and delimited by dashed lines. The best MCMs for q = 2 and q = 3 correspond to the same partition. The value of the log-evidence is indicated for each component. The log-evidence of the MCM (reported in Table 2) is the sum of the values of its components. Bottom. Scatter plot of the log-evidence of MCMs for all possible partitions of the basis variables, for q = 2 (along the horizontal axis) against, respectively, q = 3, 4 and 5 (along the vertical axis). Each dot corresponds to one partition, whose color indicates the number of parts, i.e., the number nICCs of ICCs of the corresponding MCMs. In each plot, the partition corresponding to the MCM with the largest log-evidence is identified by a red circle for each q; they are the best MCMs shown in the top panel. The grey circles indicate the partitions corresponding to the best MCMs for smaller values of q. The log-evidence of MCMs corresponding to the same partition decreases with q, due to the increase in complexity penalty. In particular, no partition lies above the (x = y)-line (indicated by the shaded area) and the vertical distance between this line and a dot corresponds to the increase in penalty in the log-evidence when changing q from 2 to, respectively, 3, 4, or 5 for the corresponding partition. MCMs with ICCs of the same sizes are penalized by the same amount and corresponds to aligned dots parallel to the (x = y)-line. For the MCMs with nICCs = 2 (orange dots), we indicated the size of the ICCs near the alignment: for example “[4, 5]” denotes MCMs with one ICC of size 4 and one of size 5. Models with fewer ICCs have a larger average ICC size and thus get a stronger penalty with increasing q (see orange dots moving faster down than other dots from one panel to the next).

Table 1: Discretization schemes for the Big Five Personality Test data. In the original dataset, the answers xi to the i-th statement can take five different values: 1 (disagree), 2 (slightly disagree), 3 (neutral/no opinion), 4 (slightly agree), and 5 (agree). The table gives the two mapping schemes we used between the values of the original variable xi and the new variable αi for each value of q, where x̄i and σi are respectively the empirical average and the standard deviation of xi and ϵ is a parameter.

Figure 14: MCM analysis of the Big Five Personality Test data [54] for varying values of q. a) Illustration of the two discretization schemes described in Table 1. b) Best MCMs found in the original basis of the data for each discretization scheme for q = 2, 3, and 5. The dots (some numbered) correspond to the 50 variables αi associated with the answers to the 50 questions ordered (clockwise) as in the original dataset [54]: questions 1-10 assess Extraversion (mostly in purple), questions 11-20 Emotional stability (mostly in orange), questions 21-30 Agreeableness (mostly in blue), questions 31-40 Conscientiousness (mostly in yellow), and questions 41-50 Openness to experience (mostly in red). Each colored triangle represents an ICC. The absolute value of the log-evidence for each ICC is indicated near each triangle in qits per variable per datapoint. This value is between 0 and 1, and the smaller the value the stronger the compression.

Table 2: Log-evidence values of MCMs for the US Supreme Court voting data. Raw values (in nats) of the log-evidence of the MCMs found for the US Supreme Court voting data at different values of q and the corresponding absolute values expressed in qits per datapoint. These latter provide an estimate of the complexity of the data (see Sec. 5.5), which can be interpreted as the average number of qits per datapoint needed to encode the data using MCMs.

Table 3: Log-evidence values of MCMs for the Big Five Personality Test data (with N = 602 591 datapoints). Raw value of the log-evidence in nats (first column) and absolute values of the log-evidence in qits per datapoints (second column). This latter value gives the average number of qits per datapoint needed to express the dataset using the best MCM (this is a value between 0 and n = 50), which can be thought of as giving an estimate of the complexity of the data.
